structure.title: Act I, scene 1 · A condemned father tells a shipwreck story
structure.text: Before anyone laughs at a case of mistaken identity, Egeon explains how two pairs of twins were separated. He has until evening to find the money that might save his life in Ephesus. The comedy has a deadline from the beginning.

structure.title: Act I, scene 2 – Act III · The town recognises its visitors
structure.text: Antipholus of Syracuse arrives with his servant Dromio. Local people know their faces and expect them to pay bills, return home and remember promises. Their resident twins meanwhile discover that perfectly good claims on a door or a dinner can suddenly fail.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · The private errors go public
structure.text: A chain, a debt and a locked door attract officials, neighbours and an attempted cure. By the time the duke can hear witnesses, half the town has an honest account that contradicts somebody else's honest account.

people.name: The two Dromios
people.text: They are sent to fetch money, deliver messages and do whatever the last master ordered. An audience can see why carrying out an instruction invites an inexplicable beating from the next man with the same face.

people.name: Adriana and Luciana
people.text: Adriana believes her husband neglects her. Luciana has advice about patience. Being courted by a man she believes to be her sister's husband makes that advice suddenly uncomfortable to administer.

context.title: Names by city
context.text: Syracuse and Ephesus identify which Antipholus and which Dromio we are following. The city names belong to our advantage as readers. A wife opening her door has no such label to consult.

notice.text: Track the gold chain as a piece of credit.
notice.why: Several people have sound business reasons for demanding money or delivery. A joke about who has a necklace can put a man's freedom at risk.

notice.text: Who has to absorb the error physically?
notice.why: Masters tend to explain contradictions by beating servants. The Dromios' inventiveness with a pun is one of the few resources they can deploy immediately.

opening: A stranger arrives in Ephesus and discovers that people know his name, expect his money, and hold him responsible for things he has never done. Somewhere in the city is the identical twin he has lost, accompanied by a servant who also has an identical twin. Shakespeare makes the confusion wonderfully excessive, then lets it disturb things that matter: a wife's trust, a merchant's reputation, a man's confidence that he is sane. Everyone has evidence, and almost nobody has an explanation that fits it.
